entries.title: 笔迹 script/notes
entries.shortDescription: Working fragments, notations, and studies on handwriting, stroke gestures, and the physical tempo of writing.
entries.fullText: [title]笔迹 script/notes[/title] looks at 18 years worth of hand-copied and hand-annotated scores from Shu's collection. Through observing and re-presenting these markings, she considers the way language and customs are developed in social groups and how it borrows and evolves from existing and adjacent communities.

entries.title: 述书 / SS: between books & libraries
entries.medium: Research, publishing, reading sessions, library interventions
entries.shortDescription: A long-term project traversing books, public and independent libraries, reader communities, personal collections, and reading sessions.
entries.fullText:
The name draws upon *Shu Shu* (述书)—recounting, narrating, or commenting on books—while positioning the work in the interval between books as bound objects and libraries as collective spatial institutions.

It encompasses:
- **Books**: Printed matter, artists' publications, annotated volumes, and marginalia.
- **Libraries**: Independent archives, institutional collections, public reading rooms, and personal shelves.
- **People & Conversations**: Readers, custodians, transcribers, and librarians.
- **Programmes**: Reading groups, including the [[part-time-book-club]], translation circles, and collective reading aloud.

entries.title: Part Time Book Club
entries.medium: Collective reading sessions, shared marginalia, reading lists
entries.shortDescription: Informal, periodic gatherings around reading, printed matter, and shared marginalia, developed within 述书 / SS.
entries.fullText:
An informal reading collective convened on a "part-time" basis, resisting the professionalization of reading and creating non-coercive spaces for close study.

Participants bring books, unread essays, or fragments to read alongside one another. The club explores reading as a physical, shared occupation rather than an isolated intellectual test.

Organized as part of [[ss-between-books-and-libraries]] and informed by practices of [[scores]] and collective recitation.

entries.title: scores
entries.shortDescription: Instructional diagrams, reading sequences, and choreographies for voice, eyes, or hand.
entries.fullText:
The score (谱, pu) functions in this practice not merely as musical notation, but as an open script for action, observation, and time-keeping.

A score can be:
- A typographic layout directing the eye's wandering speed
- An invitation for two strangers to share silence
- A sequence of physical constraints for transcription

Entries engaging with scores include [[thank-you-for-your-time]], [[mofang-yaoxiang-ruge]], and [[instructional-scores-pdf]].

entries.title: copying
entries.shortDescription: Copying as an embodied method of close looking, critical proximity, and cognitive transcription rather than mechanical reproduction.
entries.fullText:
Copying (临摹 linmo / 抄录 chaolu) is considered here as an active epistemic tool.

By tracing another's words, strokes, or cadence, the copyist inhabits the original text from the inside. The divergence—the involuntary tremble, the slight misreading, the fatigue of the wrist—reveals the boundary between the original and the self.

Connects deeply to [[mofang-yaoxiang-ruge]], [[script-notes]], and the archival ethos of [[ss-between-books-and-libraries]].

entries.title: in the aisle
entries.medium: Photo series, Wheat pasting and Zine installation
entries.shortDescription: in the aisle gathers photographs, textures and overheard conversations from Chinese supermarkets in Edinburgh.
entries.fullText: in the aisle gathers photographs, textures and overheard conversations from Chinese supermarkets in Edinburgh. Made during a two-week programme while living away from Singapore, the work looks at how familiar products, languages, smells and everyday exchanges can make an unfamiliar place briefly feel like home. Bringing these fragments together through photographs, wheat-pasted prints and newsprint, the work considers the supermarket not only as a place to buy things, but as a space where familiarity and community are quietly reproduced.

entries.title: things we held and grazed
entries.medium: Photo series, Newsprint and Binder clips
entries.shortDescription: Over fifteen weeks in Chicago, things we held and grazed follows discarded objects left along the streets.
entries.fullText:
Over fifteen weeks in Chicago, things we held and grazed follows discarded objects left along the streets. Many are things that once came into intimate contact with the body—things we ate from, drank from, held and touched. Some remained in the same place for weeks, each re-encounter more uncanny and begging to be photographed. The work traces these objects after their usefulness has ended, lingering on the strange distance between something once held close and something subsequently left behind.

Things that accompanied us.
Things that fed us.
Things that served us.

Things that we left.
Things that we used.
Things that we forgot.

entries.title: 互 deviations
entries.shortDescription: 互 deviations is a looping moving image in which fragments of waves converge, overlap and dissolve into new forms.
entries.fullText: 互 deviations is a looping moving image in which fragments of waves converge, overlap and dissolve into new forms. Accompanied by a digitally constructed soundscape of the sea, the work moves between images that feel familiar yet difficult to place: coastline, body, surface, movement. Emerging from experiments made during 临摹 Lapping Emulations, it considers how repetition and recombination can produce an image that continually shifts away from its source.

entries.title: 临摹 Lapping Emulations
entries.medium: Experimental processes, Prints and Moving images
entries.shortDescription: 临摹 Lapping Emulations is a process-led body of prints and moving images exploring imitation as a way of making images and understanding identity.
entries.fullText:
临摹 Lapping Emulations is a process-led body of prints and moving images exploring imitation as a way of making images and understanding identity. Developed through improvised darkroom and editing processes, images of coastlines and personal objects are repeatedly copied, altered and recombined until their sources become unstable.
Made while thinking through my Henghua and Singaporean Chinese identity, the work approaches culture in a similar way: not as something fixed or inherited intact, but something continually reproduced and reshaped. The sea recurs throughout the work as both image and method—a form without fixed boundaries, continually changed by movement, contact and return.

entries.title: national flower
entries.shortDescription: national flower is an affectionate study of the bougainvillea scattered across Singapore's landscape.
entries.fullText: national flower is an affectionate study of the bougainvillea scattered across Singapore's landscape. Begun during the pandemic through walks taken on Google Maps Street View, the work collects the recurring patches of pink, magenta and fuchsia that appear along roads, fences and edges of the city. Ubiquitous but easily overlooked, these flowers form an unofficial image of Singapore, which leads to the playful proposition that perhaps these are our real national flowers.

entries.title: 回 kuala
entries.shortDescription: 回 kuala begins with a childhood memory of a teapot-shaped landmark on the journey to my father's hometown in Brunei.
entries.fullText:
回 kuala begins with a childhood memory of a teapot-shaped landmark on the journey to my father's hometown in Brunei. I was too young to photograph it then, and more than two decades later, what remains is a vivid but increasingly uncertain image in my mind.
Working with 66 photographs of the landmark found online, I repeatedly process and erode other people's images in an attempt to approach my own. Rather than reconstructing the landmark more clearly, the images become increasingly unstable—somewhere between photographic evidence and remembered image.
回 kuala is an experiment in photographing a memory when a photograph was never taken.

印象深刻的茶壶雕塑在我记忆中是朦胧的。它是跟着我爸爸回汶莱的路上一定会经过的地标。
我记得最后一次看到茶壶应该有二十年前了，听说茶壶的装饰灯已经坏了，时钟也停了。

I remember seeing the teapot over two decades ago, and rumor has it that the lights and clocks on it have already stopped working a few years ago.

entries.title: 默契 sync
entries.shortDescription: 默契 sync takes the ritual of pre-concert tuning as a way of thinking about synchronisation within an orchestra.
entries.fullText:
默契 sync takes the ritual of pre-concert tuning as a way of thinking about synchronisation within an orchestra. Before performing, musicians listen and adjust to one another, producing the impression of a single ensemble coming into tune.
The work separates this collective act into individual measurements. Lines extracted from electronic tuner readings of different orchestras overlap on screen, only occasionally meeting at the “correct” pitch. A five-channel soundtrack resembles an orchestra tuning together, but is assembled from musicians individually tuning their instruments to a machine rather than to one another.
默契  (mò qì, meaning a tacit understanding or rapport) asks how much collective synchronisation is actually shared, and how much is something we perceive or construct.

entries.title: 再见阿炳 who is abing?
entries.shortDescription: 再见阿炳 who is abing?
entries.fullText:
再见阿炳 who is abing? begins with the only known surviving photograph of Abing, the influential blind folk musician and erhu player. Despite this single visual reference, his likeness has been repeatedly reimagined through illustrations, sculptures, reenactments and user-made videos.
The work gathers these representations into a continuous strip, tracing how one image has been copied, interpreted and embellished over time. Across them, certain features recur while others drift, contributing to a familiar image of the erhu player that extends beyond Abing himself.
The work considers how a likeness is constructed when there is almost nothing to copy from.

entries.title: 音情圆缺 phases
entries.shortDescription: 音情圆缺 phases gathers images of the moon found in online videos of Erquan Yingyue (二泉映月, Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring).
entries.fullText:
音情圆缺 phases gathers images of the moon found in online videos of Erquan Yingyue (二泉映月, Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring). Across professional performances, amateur recordings and user-made videos, the moon repeatedly appears as a visual shorthand for the music—photographed, illustrated, animated and composited in different ways.
Extracted from their original videos and presented on lightboxes, these moons form a collection of how the same image has been imagined again and again. Like the moon, which is visible through reflected sunlight, these digital moons only appear when illuminated: first by the computer screen, and again by the lightbox.

entries.title: 尘惦 chen dian (found on paper, made in minds)
entries.medium: Lightboxes and Improvisations from graphical scores
entries.shortDescription: 尘惦 chen dian (found on paper, made in minds) begins with used Chinese orchestra scores: hand-copied, annotated, repeatedly photocopied and passed between musicians.
entries.fullText:
尘惦 chen dian (found on paper, made in minds) begins with used Chinese orchestra scores: hand-copied, annotated, repeatedly photocopied and passed between musicians. Enlarged and illuminated, their markings and printing artefacts reveal traces accumulated through use and circulation.
Taking Liu Tianhua's 空山鸟语 (Birdsongs in the Vacant Valley) as a point of departure, these visual traces are also read as graphical scores for new improvisations. Marks that once accompanied the learning and sharing of music are returned to sound, allowing one generation of notation, copying and use to prompt another act of interpretation.

entries.medium: Found notation, Archival inkjet print on Canson Rag

Isolated from their original context, these “non-notes” form an almost-graphical score, suspended between something to be read, seen and performed.

entries.title: 迁泉 shifting springs
entries.shortDescription: 迁泉 shifting springs begins with Huishan's Second Spring (天下第二泉), historically celebrated for the quality of its water for tea and later closely associated with Abing, who played 二泉映月 (Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring) there.
entries.fullText:
迁泉 shifting springs begins with Huishan's Second Spring (天下第二泉), historically celebrated for the quality of its water for tea and later closely associated with Abing, who played 二泉映月 (Mirrored Moon in the Erquan Spring) there. Today, the spring has largely dried up, leaving a place whose cultural image persists beyond its water.
The work turns to amateur and professional videos found online, where the spring continues to flow, reappear and be reimagined. Through experimental prints and video objects, these images are processed and displaced, tracing how a place can persist through music, memory and circulating images even as its physical form changes.

泉里的水干了以后，留下的是“白”——空白的白。没有了水，泉反而成了一个可以不断被想象、填补的地方。记忆、音乐和流传的影像在这片空白里交叠，让已经消失的水一次次重新流动。
网上的影像也是如此。不同的人拍摄、上传、转发，又重新想象同一个泉。久而久之，这些影像像一个由大众共同累积的时间囊：泉水或许已经干了，但关于它的想象还在流动。

entries.title: 乍鸣 creak of dawn
entries.medium:
Montage of self-recorded and found field recordings of birds at sunrise
30’42”
entries.shortDescription: 乍鸣 creak of dawn gathers self-recorded and found recordings of birds at sunrise into a 30-minute sound work.
entries.fullText:
乍鸣 creak of dawn gathers self-recorded and found recordings of birds at sunrise into a 30-minute sound work. 

I remember this phrase "日出而作 日落而息": to work when the sunrises, rest when the sunsets. Taking from the phrase, this work looks beyond hours and minutes towards environmental ways of marking time. Layered together, the recordings form a cacophonous dawn: a day announced not by a clock, but by birds.

entries.title: 一笔一勾 in two strokes
entries.shortDescription: 一笔一勾 in two strokes follows the many uses of a simple arrow found across annotated musical scores.
entries.fullText: 一笔一勾 in two strokes follows the many uses of a simple arrow found across annotated musical scores. A line with a pointed head might indicate phrasing, fingering, rhythm, which note to play, or a change in the order of a passage. Collected across different scores and contexts, the work looks at how an ordinary mark becomes a flexible musical language. I love how something drawn in two strokes can do and mean so much.

entries.title: 横竖横竖横 keeping count
entries.shortDescription: 横竖横竖横 keeping count begins with 正, a five-stroke character commonly used as a tally.
entries.fullText:
横竖横竖横 keeping count begins with 正, a five-stroke character commonly used as a tally. In my music notebooks, each stroke marked an instance of practice, slowly completing the character over time.
As a student, I once filled in the tally without having practised. My teacher caught me and remarked that if I continued like this, the only thing I was practising was how to write 正.
The diptych takes this reprimand literally. One image reproduces an uneven 正 from an old practice notebook, its five strokes written at different moments. Alongside it is a collection of characters written repeatedly in a single sitting, paced against an increasingly fast metronome: practising the act of keeping count rather than the instrument it was meant to account for.

entries.title: on telling time in the mall
entries.shortDescription: on telling time in the mall observes the different ways time makes itself visible in Queensway Shopping Centre, one of Singapore's oldest surviving malls.
entries.fullText:
on telling time in the mall observes the different ways time makes itself visible in Queensway Shopping Centre, one of Singapore's oldest surviving malls. Moving between field recordings, found footage and fly-on-the-wall observations, the video looks for time beyond the clock: shutters opening and closing, shops changing hands, repeated routines, ageing interiors and small movements that mark the passing of a day.
Bringing footage from different periods into the same cycle, the work asks how we tell that time has passed in a place where so much seems to repeat itself.

entries.shortDescription: in the aisle gathers photographs, textures and fragments of overheard conversation collected from Chinese supermarkets in Edinburgh.
entries.fullText:
in the aisle gathers photographs, textures and fragments of overheard conversation collected from Chinese supermarkets in Edinburgh. Made while living away from Singapore, the work follows these spaces through the familiar products, languages, smells and everyday exchanges that briefly made somewhere foreign feel like home.
The work takes the form of a newsprint publication, drawing from the free newspapers and distribution kiosks commonly found in these supermarkets. By borrowing a format already circulating within the space, the book considers the supermarket not only as a place to buy familiar things, but as a place where information, conversation and a sense of community are exchanged.

entries.shortDescription: 临摹 – 序 (linmo – sketches) gathers the experiments, readings and fragments that developed alongside 临摹 Lapping Emulations.
entries.fullText:
临摹 – 序 (linmo – sketches) gathers the experiments, readings and fragments that developed alongside 临摹 Lapping Emulations. Collaged photographs and texts move between darkroom experiments, family histories, research into the Chinese diaspora in Southeast Asia, and recurring images of the sea.

Rather than resolving these materials into a single account of identity, the book retains the uncertainty of the research process. Images are copied, altered and revisited, while the sea becomes a recurring way of thinking about culture as something inherited yet continually shifting.

Borrowing the words of Kuo Pao Kun, linmo – sketches is just the journal of another "cultural orphan".

entries.shortDescription: During the pandemic, I took walks around Singapore using Google Maps Street View.
entries.fullText:
During the pandemic, I took walks around Singapore using Google Maps Street View. Again and again, patches of pink, magenta and fuchsia appeared at the edges of roads and in my imagined peripheral vision.
Collected into a small accordion book, these images form an affectionate portrait of the bougainvillea scattered throughout Singapore's landscape.
These are the real national flowers of Singapore.

entries.title: 尘惦 chéndiàn; after scans and lingering dust
entries.shortDescription: 尘惦 chéndiàn; after scans and lingering dust begins with hand-copied Chinese music scores repeatedly photocopied for circulation.
entries.fullText:
尘惦 chéndiàn; after scans and lingering dust begins with hand-copied Chinese music scores repeatedly photocopied for circulation. With each generation, handwritten marks, dust and printing artefacts are copied alongside the music: some traces intensify while others slowly disappear.
The scores are scanned, enlarged, inverted and Risograph printed, turning these incidental traces into images in their own right. Each book contains 43 images selected from a larger set of 127 and is bound to stand upright like a calendar, allowing it to be read slowly over time.
The title plays between 沉淀, to settle or precipitate, and 尘惦, an invented pairing that suggests dust and something that continues to linger in the mind.

entries.title: 天明日月奣 i’ve never met yoko ono, nor have i touched the sky
entries.medium: Miniature photocards, transparent folder and oversized book belt
entries.shortDescription: 天明日月奣 / i've never met yoko ono, nor have i touched the sky collects images of the sky from photographic documentation of Yoko Ono's Sky TV (1966–2007) and TV to See the Sky (2021).
entries.fullText:
天明日月奣 / i've never met yoko ono, nor have i touched the sky collects images of the sky from photographic documentation of Yoko Ono's Sky TV (1966–2007) and TV to See the Sky (2021).
Printed as miniature photocards rather than a fixed sequence, the images can be rearranged, carried, given to a friend or held against the actual sky. The book plays with one of photography's most familiar subjects—the sky that is endlessly photographed.
Its Chinese title borrows an unattributed wordplay in which the characters for sky, sun and moon are rearranged to form 天明日月奣: clear skies, clear skies.

entries.title: what used to be in the mall
entries.shortDescription: what used to be in the mall gathers newspaper clippings about Queensway Shopping Centre from the 1970s to the 1990s.
entries.fullText:
what used to be in the mall gathers newspaper clippings about Queensway Shopping Centre from the 1970s to the 1990s. Reports, advertisements and small announcements recall a mall shaped by changing ideas of shopping, nightlife, crime, novelty and entertainment.
Printed on tracing paper and rivet-bound into a small volume, fragments from different decades sit over and through one another. Made as a companion to on telling time in the mall, the book approaches the mall's history through the incidental record left behind in newspapers—what happened there, what was sold there, and what once seemed worth reporting.

entries.title: 花·瓶·画 flower, vases, paintings and other observations
entries.shortDescription: 花·瓶·画 flower, vases, paintings and other observations collects recurring details from official and amateur erhu music videos: flower arrangements, porcelain vases, scroll paintings and other objects used to stage the performance.
entries.fullText:
花·瓶·画 flower, vases, paintings and other observations collects recurring details from official and amateur erhu music videos: flower arrangements, porcelain vases, scroll paintings and other objects used to stage the performance.
Many of the source videos, particularly from the 1980s and 1990s, have been copied and reposted repeatedly. Their colours fade, details blur and compression artefacts accumulate, yet the same visual motifs continue to circulate and be reproduced.
Rearranging these fragments in an accordion book, the work observes how repetition across staging, performance and digital copying has contributed to a familiar visual language for “Chinese music".

about.title: Hong Shu-ying 方舒颖 (b. 1997)
about.artistName: hoards images and stories to make sense of how things are learned and passed on.
about.biography:
Working across moving images, prints, and printed matter, her practice begins with images, notations and other vernacular working documents in circulation. She is interested in the drifts, contradictions and adaptations that allow shared ways of knowing and working to remain legible as they pass through different hands and contexts.

She grew up in amateur Chinese orchestras, where learning took place through photocopied scores, handwritten annotations and imitation. Alongside this, she spent her teenage years collecting and reposting images online. These parallel habits shaped how she looks at vernacular working documents—not simply as records, but as evidence of how information, knowledge and conventions are continually transmitted, adjusted and kept alive through use.

items.text: This curiosity extends beyond the studio. She co-founded Part Time Book Club, an informal collective that expands public access to art books through gatherings and exchanges. In response to limited access to formal residencies and the demands of international travel, she also initiated |      | on paper, a resource-lean residency centred on conversations and four sheets of A4 paper, grounded in the belief that meaningful artistic exchange can grow from modest resources.

Hong Shu-ying received the Kwek Leng Joo Prize of Excellence in Photography and was featured in the 6th Women in Film and Photography Showcase by Objectifs Centre for Photography and Film (SG). She has presented solo exhibitions at Esplanade (SG, 2024) and Yao Alternative Art Space 窯座 (TW, 2024), with an upcoming presentation at RM Gallery (NZ, 2026). Her work has also been shown at Three Shadows Xiamen Photography Art Centre and Pingyao International Photography Festival (CN); Jakarta International Photography Festival (IN); PRINTROOM (NL); CICA Museum (KR); Pon Ding 朋丁 (TW); and DECK, I_S_L_A_N_D_S Peninsula, Art Outreach, and ADM Gallery (SG). She holds a BFA (Hons) in Media Art (Photography) from the School of Art, Design and Media, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She was recently a resident at the Singapore Art Museum.

items.title: 1] I think of copying as an imperfect system.
items.text: No copy is ever identical to what came before it, yet copies continue to function. A blurred photocopy remains readable. A contradictory instructional diagram still teaches. A handwritten annotation continues to direct a performance. Rather than treating these differences as failures of reproduction, I am interested in how images and notations keep working through the gaps, mistranslations and contradictions that emerge between copies.

items.title: 2] My work begins with vernacular working documents:
items.text: notations, annotations, instructional diagrams, mass printed media and found images shaped by everyday practices of use. I am drawn to them and hoard them before I know why. They are not neutral records. They carry the traces of circulation and of decisions made to keep them usable. Their surfaces bear the marks of handling, correction, repetition and interpretation, evidence that they have passed through many hands before I held them in mine.

items.title: 3] Rather than extracting them from their original contexts, I borrow from the systems of copying and translation already embedded within them:
items.text: a photocopying protocol, a tracing method, a convention of annotation, a cataloguing system, an indexing structure, a compression standard, an editing strategy, a publishing format.  I work with these documents first as images, reading them photographically even when I no longer use a camera. A flatbed scanner or a screenshot suits this because it refuses the distinction between document and image. A conductor's score, a handwritten note, a GPS photodome and a newspaper clipping all become flat images, entering the same visual field before being reinterpreted through procedures inherited from their own histories.

items.title: 4] This understanding grew from nearly two decades inside amateur Chinese orchestras.
items.text: I eventually served as scores librarian. My role was to maintain the scores cabinet: counting parts, photocopying missing copies, incorporating corrections from rehearsals, and preparing versions that could still be played when we had limited instruments or musicians. Scores were rarely stable. They accumulated annotations, revisions and practical adaptations, sometimes becoming so extensively reworked that they effectively became new master copies.

items.title: 5] Learning rarely took place through pristine scores.
items.text: Techniques were acquired by watching, listening and imitating, and even the notation adapted. In the orchestras I grew up in, we knew a pair of annotation symbols as turtle and dollar sign rather than by their original [Italian] names, because the old names made less sense to a roomful of children learning from borrowed conventions. The symbols stayed useful because the people using them adapted them.

items.title: 6] Meaning does not simply move away from an origin.
items.text: It is continually adjusted by the people who need it to remain usable. What interests me are these quiet acts of maintenance, which let shared systems of knowing and working carry on as they pass through different hands, gathering small contradictions, adaptations and new ways of being understood.
